◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every analytics engineering job runs on a cloud data warehouse. Understanding why they replaced traditional databases — and what that architectural shift unlocked — is the foundation for everything else in this course. Pick wrong (or stay with on-prem) and your analytics will be slow, expensive, and outgrown within a year.

The old world: traditional databases for analytics

Before ~2015, analytics ran on the same database technology that ran apps — Oracle, SQL Server, Postgres, MySQL. These are OLTP (online transaction processing) systems built for fast row-level reads/writes powering applications.

Painful realities of using OLTP for analytics:

  • Storage and compute coupled — to add query power, you had to add storage too (and vice versa)
  • Scaling = downtime — vertical scaling required restarting; horizontal scaling was rare
  • Production database vs analytics — long queries blocked app traffic; teams ran nightly replicas
  • Row-oriented storage — fast for "get this one customer", slow for "sum all sales"
  • Capacity planning — buy hardware for peak; idle most of the year; expensive

The shift: separation of storage and compute

THE BIG IDEA
Storage and compute as INDEPENDENT services.

Data lives in cheap object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob).
Compute spins up on demand, reads from storage, returns results.
Scale either dimension independently. 
# Old world (coupled):
[Database server: 64GB RAM, 16 cores, 5TB SSD]
 ↓ contains BOTH data AND compute power
 ↓ scale up = buy bigger box; scale down = ... impossible

# New world (decoupled):
[Cheap object storage: petabytes available, ~$23/TB/month]
        ↑
        | (queries read from storage)
        ↑
[Compute cluster A]  [Compute cluster B]  [Compute cluster C]
 - autoscaling       - autoscaling        - paused (no cost)
 - pay per second    - pay per second
 - resize freely     - resize freely

Why this matters in practice

Capability Traditional DB Cloud Warehouse
Scale storage Buy bigger disks Automatic, infinite
Scale compute Restart with bigger box Resize in seconds
Concurrent workloads Compete for resources Separate clusters, no contention
Idle cost Full ($$$ even when unused) Storage only (~$23/TB)
Setup time Weeks (procurement, install) Minutes (sign up, run SQL)

The big three cloud warehouses

  • Snowflake — independent (multi-cloud); the most adopted; clean separation of compute "warehouses"
  • BigQuery — Google Cloud; truly serverless (no warehouses to manage); pay per query
  • Databricks — lakehouse model; built on Apache Spark; popular for data eng + ML

Plus secondary: AWS Redshift (legacy MPP), Microsoft Fabric / Synapse, ClickHouse Cloud, MotherDuck (DuckDB cloud).

Elastic scaling — the killer feature

# Scenario: nightly dbt run + ad-hoc analyst queries during the day

# Old world:
# - One database, sized for peak load
# - Nightly run starves analysts during the day
# - Or: idle 80% of the time

# Cloud warehouse:
# Create two compute clusters:
# - ANALYTICS_DEV (small, auto-suspend after 5 min) for analysts
# - DBT_PROD (X-large, scheduled 2am-4am) for nightly run
# - Or even: ad-hoc auto-scaling on burst

# Each compute reads the SAME storage. No data duplication.
# Pay only for compute time used.

Time travel and zero-copy clone

Two features unique to cloud warehouses (free with separation of storage/compute):

# Time travel (Snowflake example)
SELECT * FROM customers AT(TIMESTAMP => '2025-05-15 10:00:00');
# Query a table AS IT WAS at a moment in the past
# Available for default 1 day; configurable up to 90 days
# Saved your bacon when someone runs DELETE without WHERE

# Zero-copy clone
CREATE DATABASE prod_copy CLONE prod;
# Instant. Costs nothing additional.
# Independent metadata pointing to the same storage.
# Modifications to clone diverge from prod.
# Great for dev/staging environments.

SQL stays the SQL you know

Cloud warehouses speak SQL. Dialect differences exist (Snowflake vs BigQuery syntax for arrays, dates, etc.) but the core SQL is the same as Postgres or any other DB. The transition is operational, not linguistic.

★ WHY CLOUD WAREHOUSES MADE DBT POSSIBLE

The ELT pattern (load raw, transform in warehouse) only became practical because cloud warehouses can scan billions of rows in seconds. Before cloud warehouses, you HAD to transform externally because the warehouse was too slow. Now: load everything, transform with dbt. The whole modern data stack runs on this assumption.

When NOT to use a cloud warehouse

  • Real-time operational queries — sub-second app queries; use OLTP
  • Small data + low budget — Postgres is free; CDW has minimums
  • Compliance constraints — sometimes data can't leave on-prem
  • Sub-second analytical queries — consider ClickHouse / Apache Druid

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Columnar storage is THE technical reason cloud warehouses are 10-100x faster than traditional databases for analytics. Understanding how it works lets you write better queries, design better tables, and predict performance — instead of being surprised by mystery slowdowns.

Row-oriented vs column-oriented storage

The fundamental design choice in any database: how to physically arrange data on disk.

# Logical table (what you see):
| order_id | customer_id | amount | created_at          |
| 1001     | C42         | 89.97  | 2025-05-15 14:23:01 |
| 1002     | C42         | 19.99  | 2025-05-15 14:30:15 |
| 1003     | C18         | 59.98  | 2025-05-16 08:15:00 |

# Row storage (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server):
# All values for row 1 stored together, then row 2, then row 3
disk: [1001|C42|89.97|2025-05-15 14:23:01][1002|C42|19.99|2025-05-15 14:30:15][1003|C18|59.98|...]

# Column storage (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift):
# All values for column 1 stored together, then column 2, then column 3
disk: order_id:    [1001, 1002, 1003]
       customer_id: [C42, C42, C18]
       amount:      [89.97, 19.99, 59.98]
       created_at:  [2025-05-15 14:23:01, 2025-05-15 14:30:15, 2025-05-16 08:15:00]

Why columnar wins for analytics

Analytical queries usually read a few columns from many rows:

# Typical analytical query:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount)
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id;

# Row storage: must read ENTIRE row (all columns) for each row
# Even if the query only needs 3 columns of a 50-column table
# Wasted I/O reading columns you'll throw away

# Column storage: read only the columns the query touches
# Skip the other 47 columns entirely
# 10-50x less I/O

Why columnar wins for compression

A single column's values tend to be similar — same data type, often repeating. This compresses incredibly well.

# status column: ['pending', 'completed', 'completed', 'pending', 'completed', 'cancelled', ...]
# Run-length encoding: ['pending':1, 'completed':2, 'pending':1, 'completed':1, 'cancelled':1, ...]
# Dictionary encoding: store 4 unique values, then array of integers
# Result: 100x compression often

# customer_id column: 'C42', 'C42', 'C18', 'C53', 'C42', ...  
# Dictionary encoding compresses repeating strings to small ints

# created_at column: timestamps usually clustered, delta-encode them

# Row storage CAN'T compress as well — mixed data types in one row

Why columnar wins for vectorized execution

Once data is in columns, you can apply the same operation to many values at once using SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) CPU instructions.

# Computing SUM(amount) on a column of 1M values:

# Row-oriented engine: loop one row at a time
#   for each row: extract amount, add to sum
#   1M operations

# Column-oriented engine (vectorized):
#   load 1024 values at a time into CPU registers
#   add 1024 values simultaneously via SIMD
#   ~1000 operations total

# 1000x fewer CPU operations

The columnar trade-off

Columnar storage is great for analytics but terrible for OLTP:

Row store Column store
Read 1 column × many rows Slow (reads all) ✓ Fast
Read all columns × 1 row ✓ Fast (one disk seek) Slow (many seeks)
Insert one new row ✓ Fast (append) Slow (writes to many files)
Update one row ✓ Fast (one row) Slow (rewrites column files)
Aggregate over all rows Slow ✓ Very fast
Compress Limited ✓ 10-100x

Implications for your SQL

Columnar storage rewards certain patterns and punishes others:

# GOOD: select only what you need
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY customer_id;

# BAD: SELECT * scans every column unnecessarily
SELECT * FROM fct_orders WHERE customer_id = 'C42';
# Still requires reading all columns

# GOOD: filter on columns the warehouse can prune
SELECT * FROM fct_orders WHERE order_date >= '2025-05-01';
# If table is clustered on order_date, only relevant blocks read

# BAD: filter on uncorrelated columns
SELECT * FROM fct_orders WHERE customer_email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
# Full scan; columnar still has to read every value

Micro-partitions (Snowflake's term)

Cloud warehouses split a table into many small immutable chunks of ~16MB each. Each micro-partition stores columns separately. Metadata records the min/max of each column per micro-partition.

# A 100GB table = ~6,500 micro-partitions
# Each MP holds (e.g.) 20,000 rows × all 50 columns

# Query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = '2025-05-15'

# Warehouse looks at metadata:
# - MP #1: order_date min=2024-12-31, max=2025-01-04 → SKIP
# - MP #2: order_date min=2025-01-04, max=2025-01-09 → SKIP
# - MP #517: order_date min=2025-05-14, max=2025-05-16 → READ
# - MP #518: order_date min=2025-05-16, max=2025-05-19 → SKIP
# - ...

# Only 1 micro-partition out of 6,500 actually read!
# This is the "pruning" cloud warehouses do automatically

Clustering and partitioning

To maximize pruning, organize data physically by the columns you filter on:

# Snowflake — cluster keys
CREATE TABLE fct_orders (...)
CLUSTER BY (order_date, customer_id);

# BigQuery — partition + cluster
CREATE TABLE fct_orders (...)
PARTITION BY DATE(order_date)
CLUSTER BY customer_id;

# Result: queries filtering on order_date or customer_id
# skip nearly all data — sometimes 1000x faster

Materialized views

# Pre-aggregate hot queries
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS
SELECT 
    order_date,
    SUM(amount) AS revenue,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM fct_orders
GROUP BY order_date;

# Snowflake/BigQuery auto-refresh as base table changes
# Queries that match this pattern get instant results

# Cost trade-off:
# - Storage for the MV
# - Maintenance cost on base table updates
# - Compute saved on every matching query

▸ COLUMNAR IN ACTION
# Same query on 1 billion row orders table:

# Postgres (row-oriented):
SELECT customer_segment, SUM(amount) 
FROM orders 
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01' 
GROUP BY customer_segment;

# - Full table scan: read all 50 columns × 1B rows
# - I/O: ~500GB
# - Time: 30+ minutes (or crashes)

# Snowflake (columnar):
# Same SQL
# - Read only 3 columns (order_date, customer_segment, amount)
# - Pruning: skip MPs outside date range
# - I/O: ~5GB read
# - Time: ~3 seconds

# 100x less I/O, 600x faster
# Columnar storage made this possible
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Row storage: values for a row stored together (OLTP friendly)
  • Column storage: values for a column stored together (OLAP friendly)
  • Analytics queries read few columns × many rows — columnar wins
  • Columnar compresses 10-100x because values within a column are similar
  • Vectorized execution: SIMD instructions process 1024 values at once
  • Cloud warehouses split tables into micro-partitions with per-column metadata
  • Pruning skips micro-partitions outside query filters (10-1000x speedup)
  • Clustering/partitioning by frequently-filtered columns maximizes pruning
  • SELECT only the columns you need; SELECT * defeats the column advantage

You'll typically work in one cloud warehouse for years. Picking the right one matters — but more importantly, you need to know enough about all three to navigate job descriptions, interviews, and architectural discussions. They're more similar than different, but the differences shape day-to-day work.

The three main contenders

Snowflake BigQuery Databricks
Cloud Multi (AWS/Azure/GCP) GCP only Multi (AWS/Azure/GCP)
Pricing model Compute time + storage Pay per query bytes (or flat-rate slots) DBU-hours + cloud infra

Snowflake

The market leader. Best for: organizations focused on analytics, with mixed cloud preferences, who want a polished experience.

# Key concepts:
# - Database → Schema → Table (familiar hierarchy)
# - Virtual warehouse = compute cluster (sizes XS through 6XL)
# - You start/suspend warehouses; pay per second when running
# - Auto-suspend after idle period (default 10 min)
# - Auto-resume on next query

# Example workflow:
USE WAREHOUSE dbt_dev_xs;       -- pick compute
USE DATABASE analytics_dev;
USE SCHEMA marts;

SELECT customer_segment, SUM(amount)
FROM fct_orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY 1;

# Warehouse auto-suspended after 10 min of inactivity. Resumes next query.
# Pricing: credit-based. 1 XS warehouse = 1 credit/hour

Snowflake's killer features: time travel (query data as of any moment in the past), zero-copy clone (instant clones of TB+ databases at no extra storage cost), data sharing (publish data to other Snowflake accounts without copying).

BigQuery

Google's truly serverless warehouse. Best for: GCP shops, teams that prefer no compute management, very bursty workloads.

# Key concepts:
# - Project → Dataset → Table (GCP hierarchy)
# - NO warehouses to manage; truly serverless
# - "Slots" = units of compute; can be on-demand or reserved
# - Pricing: $5 per TB scanned (on-demand) OR flat-rate slots

# Example workflow:
# Just write SQL. Google handles compute.

SELECT customer_segment, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM `my-project.analytics.fct_orders`
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_segment;

# Query previews show estimated bytes BEFORE you run
# Avoid surprise bills: SELECT specific columns; partition tables

# Pricing example:
# 100 TB table; query scans 5GB (after partition pruning) = $0.025
# vs Snowflake: minimum 1 min warehouse runtime regardless of work

BigQuery's strengths: no compute config needed, native support for nested data (STRUCT, ARRAY), tight integration with Google products (GA4, Sheets, Looker), built-in ML (BQML).

Databricks

The "lakehouse" platform. Built on Spark + Delta Lake. Best for: organizations needing data engineering + ML alongside analytics, working with unstructured data, or migrating from Spark.

# Key concepts:
# - Workspace → Catalog → Schema → Table (similar to Snowflake)
# - Data lives in Delta Lake (open format) on S3/GCS/ADLS
# - Two compute types:
#   - SQL Warehouses: for BI/SQL queries (like Snowflake warehouses)
#   - All-purpose clusters: for notebooks, ML, batch jobs

# Example workflow:
USE CATALOG analytics;
USE SCHEMA marts;

SELECT customer_segment, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM fct_orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_segment;

# SQL Warehouses look like Snowflake to analysts
# Underneath: Spark engine + Photon (vectorized C++ execution)

# Same data can be queried via:
# - SQL Warehouse (analytics)
# - Python notebook (data science)
# - Spark job (data engineering)
# - Streaming (real-time)

Databricks strengths: open format (Delta Lake, no vendor lock-in on storage), Spark for big data engineering, MLflow for ML lifecycle, ability to mix SQL/Python/Scala.

▸ ONE WAREHOUSE, THREE SQL DIALECTS
# Question: "Get monthly revenue per customer last year"

SELECT

    customer_id,
    SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM fct_orders
WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, CURRENT_DATE)
GROUP BY 1, 2;

Virtual warehouses (compute)

The compute clusters that actually run your queries. You start, stop, resize, and manage these.

# Sizes (each step ~2x the resources and cost):
# XS  → S → M → L → XL → 2XL → 3XL → 4XL → 5XL → 6XL

# Credits per hour:
# XS: 1   credit/hr
# S:  2   credits/hr
# M:  4   credits/hr
# L:  8   credits/hr
# XL: 16  credits/hr
# 2XL: 32 credits/hr
# ... doubles each size

# Auto-suspend after idle (typically 10 min)

Creating a warehouse

-- Create warehouse for analysts
CREATE WAREHOUSE ANALYST_WH
    WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'X-SMALL'
    AUTO_SUSPEND = 60                  -- pause after 60 sec idle
    AUTO_RESUME = TRUE                  -- start on next query
    INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE
    MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
    MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 3              -- multi-cluster for concurrency
    SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD';

-- Use it
USE WAREHOUSE ANALYST_WH;

-- Resize on demand (no downtime)
ALTER WAREHOUSE ANALYST_WH SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM';

-- Suspend manually
ALTER WAREHOUSE ANALYST_WH SUSPEND;

-- Check status
SHOW WAREHOUSES;

Multi-cluster warehouses

# For high concurrency (many users querying at once):

CREATE WAREHOUSE BI_WH
    WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM'
    MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
    MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 5      -- spawns extra clusters as needed
    SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD'; -- vs 'ECONOMY' (waits longer to spin up)

# How it works:
# - Single cluster handles queries up to its capacity
# - Queue forms = spawn another cluster
# - Queue drains = retire extra clusters
# - You pay only for active clusters

# Use for:
# - BI tools with many concurrent users
# - Customer-facing analytics
# Don't use for:
# - dbt runs (one workflow, sequential)
# - Single analyst queries

Sizing tips

★ WAREHOUSE SIZING HEURISTICS
  • XS: ad-hoc analyst queries, dev work, small dbt runs (less than 50 models)
  • S/M: larger dbt runs (50-200 models), heavier BI dashboards
  • L: big dbt runs (200+ models), data science batch jobs
  • XL+: very large single queries; bulk loading huge datasets

Don't oversize. A larger warehouse runs faster but proportionally more expensive — same total credits, less wall time. Right-size for your time tolerance.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before dbt can transform anything, data has to land in Snowflake. Knowing the load patterns — bulk COPY, streaming Snowpipe, external tables — lets you handle any ingest scenario. You'll mostly use Fivetran or Airbyte (which use these under the hood) but understanding the primitives lets you debug and customize.

Three ways to get data into Snowflake

LOAD PATTERNS
1. COPY INTO: bulk load files from a stage (most common)
2. Snowpipe: continuous loading as files arrive
3. External tables: query files in-place (no copy)
4. Streams + Tasks: change data capture within Snowflake
5. Direct insert: INSERT INTO (small ad-hoc only)

Stages: where files live before loading

# A stage is a location where data files live, accessible to Snowflake

# Three types:
# 1. User stage (built-in per user; @~)
# 2. Table stage (built-in per table; @%table_name)
# 3. Named stage (you create; supports external locations)

# Internal named stage (Snowflake-managed)
CREATE STAGE my_internal_stage
    FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'CSV' FIELD_DELIMITER = ',' SKIP_HEADER = 1);

# Upload files via SnowSQL CLI
PUT file:///local/path/data.csv @my_internal_stage;

# External stage (your S3/GCS bucket)
CREATE STAGE my_s3_stage
    URL = 's3://my-bucket/data/'
    STORAGE_INTEGRATION = my_s3_integration  -- IAM role
    FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'PARQUET');

# List files in a stage
LIST @my_s3_stage;

COPY INTO — bulk loading

# Basic load
COPY INTO orders
FROM @my_s3_stage/orders/2025-05-15.parquet
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'PARQUET');

# Load all files in a folder
COPY INTO orders
FROM @my_s3_stage/orders/
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'PARQUET')
PATTERN = '.*\.parquet';

# With transformation during load
COPY INTO orders (order_id, customer_id, amount_usd, created_at)
FROM (
    SELECT 
        $1:order_id::INT,
        $1:customer_id::VARCHAR,
        $1:amount_cents::NUMERIC / 100,    -- transform cents to dollars
        $1:created_at::TIMESTAMP_NTZ
    FROM @my_s3_stage/orders/2025-05-15.parquet
)
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'PARQUET');

# Error handling
COPY INTO orders
FROM @my_s3_stage/orders/
ON_ERROR = 'SKIP_FILE'              -- options: ABORT_STATEMENT (default), CONTINUE, SKIP_FILE, SKIP_FILE_n
VALIDATION_MODE = 'RETURN_ERRORS';  -- dry-run that returns errors only

File formats supported

CSV Most common. Specify delimiter, headers, NULL chars, quoting.
JSON Loaded as VARIANT; flexible nested data; one row per top-level object.
Parquet Best for analytics. Columnar, compressed, typed. Default for data lakes.
Avro Kafka pipelines; schema-evolution friendly.
ORC Hadoop legacy; similar to Parquet.
XML Rare; loaded as VARIANT.

Reusable file formats

# Define once, reuse everywhere
CREATE OR REPLACE FILE FORMAT my_csv_format
    TYPE = 'CSV'
    FIELD_DELIMITER = ','
    SKIP_HEADER = 1
    FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"'
    NULL_IF = ('NULL', 'null', '')
    EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL = TRUE
    DATE_FORMAT = 'YYYY-MM-DD'
    TIMESTAMP_FORMAT = 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS';

# Use in COPY
COPY INTO orders FROM @stage/file.csv
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'my_csv_format');

Snowpipe — continuous loading

Auto-loads files as they arrive in cloud storage. Pay per file load, not by warehouse time.

# Create a pipe
CREATE PIPE order_events_pipe
    AUTO_INGEST = TRUE
    AS
    COPY INTO order_events
    FROM @my_s3_stage/events/
    FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'my_parquet_format');

# Set up S3 event notification → SNS/SQS → Snowpipe queue
# When a new file lands in S3, Snowpipe ingests it within ~1 min

# Use cases:
# - Streaming-ish use case (sub-minute is overkill, Kafka direct is better)
# - File-based pipelines from data producers
# - Replacing nightly batch with continuous

# Pricing: per file + Snowpipe credits
# Generally cheaper than running a warehouse 24/7

External tables — query without loading

# Query Parquet/CSV in S3 directly, no copy
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE order_events_ext
    LOCATION = @my_s3_stage/events/
    FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'my_parquet_format')
    AUTO_REFRESH = TRUE;

# Query like any table
SELECT * FROM order_events_ext 
WHERE value:event_type::STRING = 'page_view';

# Pros:
# - No storage cost in Snowflake
# - Always reflects source (auto-refresh)
# - Useful for huge data lakes you don't want to copy

# Cons:
# - Slower than native Snowflake tables
# - No clustering
# - Limited optimizations

# Best for: occasional queries on cold data

Streams — change data capture in Snowflake

# Track changes on a table
CREATE STREAM orders_stream ON TABLE orders;

# Now SELECT * FROM orders_stream returns only NEW/CHANGED rows
SELECT * FROM orders_stream;

# Combined with TASK (scheduled SQL):
CREATE TASK process_orders
    WAREHOUSE = ETL_WH
    SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
    AS
    INSERT INTO orders_history
    SELECT *, METADATA$ACTION FROM orders_stream;

# Pattern: source updated → stream captures change → task processes → stream consumed
# Build incremental pipelines without external orchestrators

The Fivetran / Airbyte reality

Most companies don't write COPY INTO themselves. They use managed connectors:

# Fivetran / Airbyte do all the work:
# 1. Authenticate to source (Stripe, Salesforce, Postgres, ...)
# 2. Extract data (often via API or replication slot)
# 3. Load to Snowflake via COPY INTO under the hood
# 4. Maintain incremental sync (CDC where possible)
# 5. Handle schema drift, retries, failures

# Result: raw data appears in your warehouse continuously
# Your job: build models on top with dbt

# What to know:
# - These tools cost real money ($1k+/month for many connectors)
# - They typically land data in a schema like "stripe", "salesforce" 
# - Add _fivetran_synced / _airbyte_loaded_at columns
# - Source freshness in dbt monitors their health

When to do it yourself

  • Custom source — no connector exists (rare these days)
  • Cost optimization — high-volume sources expensive on managed tools
  • Compliance — data can't go through third party
  • Real-time — Snowpipe Streaming for sub-second

# Daily exports of order_events sit in S3 as Parquet
# We want them in Snowflake within minutes of arrival

# 1. Create the storage integration (IAM role)

    TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
    STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
    ENABLED = TRUE
    STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-s3'
    STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://my-events/');

# 2. Create the stage
CREATE STAGE events_stage
    URL = 's3://my-events/order_events/'
    STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_int
    FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = PARQUET);

# 3. Create target table
CREATE TABLE raw_order_events (
    raw VARIANT,
    loaded_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
);

# 4. Create the pipe
CREATE PIPE events_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS
COPY INTO raw_order_events (raw)
FROM (SELECT $1 FROM @events_stage);

# 5. Configure S3 → SNS → Snowpipe (in AWS console)
# Files landing in s3://my-events/order_events/ now auto-load

# 6. dbt staging model
# stg_events.sql:
SELECT
    raw:event_id::VARCHAR as event_id,
    raw:user_id::VARCHAR as user_id,
    raw:event_type::VARCHAR as event_type,
    raw:event_ts::TIMESTAMP_NTZ as event_ts,
    loaded_at
FROM {{ source('raw', 'raw_order_events') }}

Snowflake bills can spiral fast — six-figure surprise invoices are real. The pricing model

SNOWFLAKE COSTS
Storage: ~$23/TB/month (compressed) — usually cheap
Compute (credits): the big variable; charged per second of warehouse runtime
Cloud services: usually included (free up to 10% of compute)
Data transfer: egress charges if data leaves region

Warehouse sizing economics

# Each size step doubles cost AND (usually) halves runtime
# So same query costs ROUGHLY the same regardless of size

# Example: query that takes 10 min on XS
# XS (1 cr/hr): 10 min × 1/60 cr = 0.167 credits
# S  (2 cr/hr): 5 min × 2/60 cr  = 0.167 credits
# M  (4 cr/hr): 2.5 min × 4/60 cr = 0.167 credits

# WHEN bigger is better:
# - You need the result faster (analyst waiting)
# - Memory-bound query that spills to disk on smaller sizes

# WHEN smaller is better:
# - Scheduled overnight job (no one's waiting)
# - Small queries (1-min minimum negates speedup)
# - Concurrent queries (multi-cluster small > single large)

Auto-suspend — the most important setting

# Auto-suspend pauses the warehouse after N seconds of idle
# Once suspended, no compute charges (storage still counts)

ALTER WAREHOUSE ANALYST_WH SET AUTO_SUSPEND = 60;     -- 1 minute idle

# Recommended values:
# - Interactive analyst warehouses: 60 seconds
# - dbt prod warehouses: 60 seconds
# - BI tool warehouses with constant queries: longer (300-600s)
# - Never set to 0 (means "never suspend" = always running)

# The default is 600 seconds (10 minutes) — too long for cost control
# CHANGE THIS on every warehouse you create

Auto-resume

ALTER WAREHOUSE ANALYST_WH SET AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;

# When suspended, warehouse auto-starts on next query (~5-10 sec)
# Users see brief pause, then results

# Cost of resume: nothing extra
# Always enable AUTO_RESUME

Multi-cluster sizing

# For concurrent users (BI tools, analyst teams):

CREATE WAREHOUSE BI_WH
    WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM'
    MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Time travel and zero-copy clone are Snowflake's superpower features. They make recovering from mistakes cheap, cloning environments instant, and sharing data trivial. These free byproducts of separation of storage and compute change how you think about data operations.

Time Travel

Query any table AS IT WAS at any moment in the recent past. Free, automatic, built-in.

# Query a table 1 hour ago
SELECT * FROM orders AT(OFFSET => -60*60);  -- 1 hour back

# Query at a specific timestamp
SELECT * FROM orders AT(TIMESTAMP => '2025-05-15 14:00:00'::TIMESTAMP);

# Query before a specific query (statement ID)
SELECT * FROM orders BEFORE(STATEMENT => '01234567-89ab-cdef-...');

# Compare current vs prior state
SELECT 'now' AS state, COUNT(*) FROM orders
UNION ALL
SELECT '1hr ago', COUNT(*) FROM orders AT(OFFSET => -3600);

Retention period

# Default: 1 day for standard tables
# Configurable: 0-90 days (Enterprise tier and above)

# Set retention on a table
ALTER TABLE orders SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 30;

# Set at schema or database level (inherited)
ALTER SCHEMA marts SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 14;
ALTER DATABASE analytics SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 7;

# Trade-off:
# Longer retention = more storage cost
# Time travel storage costs the same as regular storage

# Recommendation:
# - Critical tables: 7-14 days
# - Marts: 1-3 days (rebuildable from staging)
# - Staging: 1 day (rebuildable from sources)
# - Snapshots: 7-30 days (recovery hard if lost)

Recovering dropped objects

# Accidentally dropped a table? Recover it
UNDROP TABLE my_important_table;

# Works on:
# - Tables
# - Schemas
# - Databases

# Must be within the retention period (or fail-safe)
# Saves your bacon when DELETE WITHOUT WHERE happens

Fail-safe

# Beyond time travel: fail-safe (7 days additional)
# - Only Snowflake support can recover
# - Free (included in storage)
# - Last-resort disaster recovery

# Total recovery window:
# Time travel (1-90 days, you control) + Fail-safe (7 days, Snowflake controls)

# Storage usage:
# active_bytes        — current data
# time_travel_bytes   — change history within retention
# failsafe_bytes      — last-7-days additional

Zero-copy clone

Instantly create an independent copy of a database, schema, or table — without duplicating storage.

# Clone a database (instant, regardless of size)
CREATE DATABASE prod_clone CLONE prod;

# Clone a single table
CREATE TABLE orders_test CLONE orders;

# Clone schema
CREATE SCHEMA marts_test CLONE marts;

# Clone at a point in time (combine with time travel)
CREATE TABLE orders_backup CLONE orders AT(TIMESTAMP => '2025-05-15 14:00:00');

# How it works:
# - Metadata copy only — clone shares storage with source
# - When clone is modified, only those changes get new storage
# - "Copy on write" semantics

# Costs:
# - Initial clone: free (just metadata)
# - Modifications: pay for changed data only

Use cases for cloning

  1. Dev/test environments — clone prod into dev_username for safe experimentation
  2. Pre-deployment validation — clone prod, run new dbt models, validate, then apply
  3. Restore from time travel — clone the table as it was, then swap
  4. Ad-hoc analysis — break off a copy to experiment without risking prod
  5. Sandboxing — give a new analyst their own clone to learn on

Recovering from a bad deployment

# Scenario: bad dbt run corrupted fct_orders
# Recover via clone + swap

-- Step 1: clone the prior state of fct_orders
CREATE TABLE fct_orders_recovered CLONE fct_orders 
AT(TIMESTAMP => '2025-05-15 06:00:00');   -- before the bad run

-- Step 2: verify it looks right
SELECT COUNT(*), MAX(order_date) FROM fct_orders_recovered;

-- Step 3: swap (atomic rename)
ALTER TABLE fct_orders SWAP WITH fct_orders_recovered;

-- Step 4: now fct_orders is the recovered version
-- And fct_orders_recovered is the broken one
-- Drop the broken version when confident:
DROP TABLE fct_orders_recovered;

# Recovery: minutes instead of hours, no data loss

Secure Data Sharing

Share read-only access to your tables with other Snowflake accounts — no copying, no ETL.

# Create a share
CREATE SHARE my_share;

# Add objects to the share
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE analytics TO SHARE my_share;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA analytics.marts TO SHARE my_share;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA analytics.marts TO SHARE my_share;

# Grant share to consumer account
ALTER SHARE my_share ADD ACCOUNTS = consumer_account;

# Consumer creates a database from your share:
CREATE DATABASE shared_analytics FROM SHARE provider_account.my_share;

# Now consumer queries the shared data live
# - No copying = always fresh
# - No storage cost for consumer
# - Provider pays only for storage; consumer pays for compute when they query

# Use cases:
# - Cross-team data sharing
# - Vendor → customer data sharing
# - Replacing nightly file exports

Snowflake Marketplace

# Browse public datasets shared by providers
# Examples: weather data, financial data, demographics

# In Snowsight: Marketplace → Browse
# Click "Get" → choose a database name → instant access
# Query in your account immediately

# Free providers: government, open data
# Paid: subscribe and pay monthly

Data Replication

# Replicate a database across regions/accounts for DR
ALTER DATABASE analytics ENABLE REPLICATION TO ACCOUNTS dr_account;

# Refresh from primary
ALTER DATABASE analytics_replica REFRESH;

# Switch over (in disaster scenario)
ALTER DATABASE analytics_replica PRIMARY;

# Use for: disaster recovery, geo-redundancy, multi-region serving

Time travel + clone + sharing together change how you think about data ops. Mistakes are reversible (clone + swap). Environments are free (clone a database). External sharing is live (no ETL). These features only exist because Snowflake separated storage from compute — the foundational architectural choice pays dividends everywhere.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

BigQuery is Google Cloud's serverless data warehouse — one of the three big players (alongside Snowflake and Redshift) you'll meet in any modern data role. Its architecture, separation of storage and compute, and (notoriously surprising) pricing model determine how you write efficient queries and how you avoid running up huge cloud bills. Understanding what's actually happening when you click "Run" makes you a far better engineer.

Serverless: no clusters, no servers

Unlike traditional warehouses where you provision a cluster (size, count, uptime), BigQuery has NO PROVISIONING. You write SQL; BigQuery allocates compute on demand from a massive shared pool ("slots"); you pay per query (or per slot-hour for flat-rate). This is the defining feature.

Separated storage and compute

Two independent systems:

  • Storage — your tables live in Google's distributed columnar store (Capacitor). Compressed and replicated automatically. Priced per GB/month.
  • Compute — when you query, BigQuery's execution engine (Dremel) scans the relevant data and runs your query. Priced per TB scanned (on-demand) or per slot-hour (flat-rate).

You can have hundreds of TB stored and pay only for storage if you never query. Or query the same data daily and pay compute every time. The two are billed independently.

Columnar storage (Capacitor)

Each column is stored separately, in its own compressed file. When you SELECT user_id, country FROM logs, BigQuery reads only the user_id and country columns — never touches the other 50 columns in the table.

This is the foundation of analytical query speed. It's also why SELECT * is the most expensive query you can write — it scans every column.

How queries execute (Dremel)

Dremel is BigQuery's query engine, evolved from a Google research project. Execution model:

  1. Parse SQL, plan the query (which tables, columns, joins, etc.)
  2. Split the work across thousands of slots (workers)
  3. Each slot reads its share of the columnar data from storage
  4. Intermediate results shuffle through a tree of aggregators
  5. Final result returns to the caller

For a simple aggregate over 1 TB, BigQuery may use 1000+ slots in parallel, finishing in seconds. This massive parallelism is why "serverless" doesn't mean "slow."

Slots — the compute unit

A slot is a unit of CPU + RAM that does part of a query. Roughly one slot ≈ one core working on data. A typical query might use 100–1000 slots in parallel. Slots are FREE on-demand (you just pay per TB scanned); you only see them on flat-rate pricing.

On-demand pricing

Default model. You pay for the BYTES SCANNED by your query:

  • $6.25 per TB scanned (as of 2026, varies by region)
  • First 1 TB per month is free
  • Caching of identical queries within 24 hours is free

BigQuery shows the estimated bytes BEFORE you run a query:

-- BigQuery UI shows: "This query will process X.X GB when run."
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*)
FROM logs
WHERE event_date = '2026-01-15'
GROUP BY user_id

The cost is predictable: bytes × price per TB. ALWAYS check the estimate before clicking Run on a big query.

Flat-rate (capacity) pricing

For high-volume customers: buy a fixed number of slots, pay a flat monthly rate, and run unlimited queries with that capacity. Predictable bills, but capacity ceiling.

Pick flat-rate when you have steady-state heavy usage. Stick with on-demand for occasional or bursty workloads.

Storage pricing

  • Active storage ($0.02/GB/month): data modified within the last 90 days
  • Long-term storage ($0.01/GB/month, half-price): data unchanged for 90+ days

BigQuery automatically moves untouched tables to long-term storage. No effort required. Queries work the same on either tier.

What makes a query expensive

  • SELECT * on wide tables — reads every column
  • No partition or cluster filter — scans the whole table
  • Large CROSS JOIN — quadratic data movement
  • UDFs in JavaScript — break the optimizer, force row-at-a-time evaluation
  • Frequent identical queries — cached for 24h, but cache misses count

Partitioning

Split a large table by date (or integer range). Queries that filter on the partition key SKIP all other partitions entirely.

CREATE TABLE logs
PARTITION BY DATE(event_time)
AS SELECT * FROM raw_logs;

-- Scans only one day's data, not the whole table:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM logs WHERE DATE(event_time) = '2026-01-15';

For a 1 TB table partitioned by day, a single-day query scans ~3 GB instead of 1 TB. 300× cheaper.

Clustering

Within each partition, sort the data by 1–4 columns. Queries that filter on the cluster keys skip blocks of irrelevant data.

CREATE TABLE logs
PARTITION BY DATE(event_time)
CLUSTER BY user_id, country
AS SELECT * FROM raw_logs;

-- Skips most user_ids quickly:
SELECT * FROM logs WHERE user_id = 'abc123' AND DATE(event_time) = '2026-01-15';

Combined partitioning + clustering can reduce scan from 1 TB to a few MB. Massive cost savings on point lookups.

Materialized views

Precomputed aggregates stored as a special table, kept up-to-date automatically. BigQuery transparently rewrites matching queries to use the materialized view instead.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_active_users AS
SELECT DATE(event_time) AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS dau
FROM logs
GROUP BY day;

Queries on daily_active_users are instant and cheap. Costs you the storage for the view + a refresh fee, but huge wins on repeated dashboards.

Streaming inserts vs batch loads

  • Batch loads (LOAD DATA, bq command, CSV/Avro/Parquet upload) — free, but minutes-to-hours latency
  • Streaming inserts (Insert API, Dataflow) — $0.01 per 200 MB; data queryable in seconds

For real-time dashboards: stream. For nightly ETL: batch (free).

Cost-control best practices

  1. Always use SELECT col1, col2 — never SELECT *
  2. Partition large tables by a date column
  3. Cluster on the most-filtered columns
  4. Use materialized views for repeated aggregates
  5. Set query cost limits per user (maximumBytesBilled)
  6. Use BI Engine reservation for dashboards if available
  7. Delete or archive cold tables you no longer need
  8. Approve >X GB queries via UI confirmation

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Partitioning and clustering are BigQuery's two most important performance and cost-reduction features. Tables without them can cost 1000x more to query. Tables with them properly applied let you query terabytes for cents. This is THE BigQuery skill that distinguishes amateurs from pros.

Partitioning

Split a table into segments based on a column's value. BigQuery scans only the partitions matching your WHERE clause.

# Partition by date column (most common)
CREATE TABLE fct_orders (
    order_id STRING,
    customer_id STRING,
    amount NUMERIC,
    order_date DATE
)
PARTITION BY order_date;

# Query that benefits:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount)
FROM fct_orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-05-01' AND '2025-05-31'  -- scans only May
GROUP BY customer_id;

# WITHOUT partition: scan ALL of fct_orders (e.g., 5 TB) = $25
# WITH partition:    scan only 1 month (e.g., 100 GB) = $0.50
# 50x savings — typical pattern

Partition types

DATE/DATETIME/TIMESTAMP Most common. Daily/monthly/yearly granularity.
INTEGER Range-based (e.g., partition by hash of user_id mod 100).
Ingestion time _PARTITIONTIME pseudo-column. Loaded-at timestamp.
No partition For small tables (<1GB); partitioning adds overhead.

Partition granularity

# Daily partitions (most common)
PARTITION BY DATE(order_ts)

# Hourly (for high-volume; max 4000 partitions total)
PARTITION BY TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(event_ts, HOUR)

# Monthly (long retention with lower volumes)
PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC(order_date, MONTH)

# Yearly (huge historical archives)
PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC(event_date, YEAR)

# Choose based on:
# - Query patterns (do you filter by day? month?)
# - Volume per period (don't over-partition)
# - Retention (long-term storage benefits from coarser)
# - 4000-partition limit per table

Clustering

Within each partition, sort data by additional columns. Lets BigQuery skip blocks within a partition.

# Partition + cluster combination
CREATE TABLE fct_orders (
    order_id STRING,
    customer_id STRING,
    product_id STRING,
    amount NUMERIC,
    order_date DATE
)
PARTITION BY order_date
CLUSTER BY customer_id, product_id;

# Query that benefits from clustering:
SELECT *
FROM fct_orders
WHERE order_date = '2025-05-15'    -- partition prune (1 day)
  AND customer_id = 'C42';          -- cluster prune (within that day)

# Without cluster: scan entire 2025-05-15 partition (e.g., 1 GB)
# With cluster:    scan only blocks containing customer_id = 'C42' (e.g., 10 MB)
# 100x additional savings on top of partitioning

# Up to 4 cluster columns; order matters (first column most useful)

When to cluster vs partition

Use partition for Date/time columns with continuous, predictable values
Use cluster for High-cardinality columns frequently filtered (customer_id, product_id, event_type)

The 1MB minimum partition issue

# Each partition incurs minimum 1MB billing
# So if you have 365 daily partitions × 1MB = 365MB minimum billed

# Don't partition tiny tables — it costs MORE than not partitioning
# Rule of thumb: partition only tables > 1 GB

# Don't partition by hour for low-volume tables — each hour = 1MB minimum
# Use day granularity unless volume justifies hour

Require partition filter

# Force users to filter by partition (prevents accidental full scans)
CREATE TABLE fct_orders (...)
PARTITION BY order_date
OPTIONS (require_partition_filter = TRUE);

# Now queries without a WHERE clause on order_date will FAIL:
SELECT * FROM fct_orders;
# Error: Cannot query over table 'fct_orders' without a filter over column(s) 'order_date'

# Must filter:
SELECT * FROM fct_orders WHERE order_date = '2025-05-15';   -- works

# Recommended for: all production fact tables > 100 GB

Partition expiration

# Auto-delete old partitions to manage storage
ALTER TABLE fct_events
SET OPTIONS (partition_expiration_days = 730);  -- 2 years

# After 2 years, partitions auto-drop
# Cheaper than manual deletion
# Combine with partition_date for retention policies

Wildcard tables (legacy pattern)

# Old pattern: one table per day with date suffix
# events_20250515, events_20250516, events_20250517, ...

# Query across many tables:
SELECT * FROM `my_project.dataset.events_*`
WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20250515' AND '20250517';

# Modern: partitioned single table > wildcard tables
# But you'll see wildcard pattern in legacy code (especially GA4 export)

Inspecting partition usage

# See partitions and sizes
SELECT 
    partition_id,
    total_rows,
    total_logical_bytes / 1e9 AS gb
FROM `my_project.analytics.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.PARTITIONS`
WHERE table_name = 'fct_orders'
ORDER BY partition_id DESC
LIMIT 30;

# Output:
# partition_id | total_rows | gb
# 20250517     | 50000      | 0.2
# 20250516     | 48000      | 0.18
# 20250515     | 52000      | 0.21
# ...

# Spot anomalies: huge partitions, missing days, unexpected data

Clustering changes

# Cluster columns can be changed without rebuild
ALTER TABLE fct_orders
SET OPTIONS (clustering_fields = ['customer_id', 'product_id', 'order_status']);

# BigQuery re-clusters in the background (free)
# Queries get more efficient as background work completes

# Partition columns CANNOT be changed (table must be rebuilt)
# So decide partition column carefully upfront
★ THE PARTITION + CLUSTER PLAYBOOK

For any fact table > 100 GB:

  1. Partition by the date column you filter on most (usually order_date / event_date)
  2. Cluster by 1-4 high-cardinality columns you often filter or join on (customer_id, product_id, event_type)
  3. Set require_partition_filter = TRUE
  4. Set partition_expiration_days if retention is finite

This combination typically reduces query costs by 10-1000x.

In dbt

    materialized='incremental',
    partition_by={
        "field": "order_date",
        "data_type": "date",
        "granularity": "day"
    },
    cluster_by=['customer_id', 'product_id'],
    require_partition_filter=true,
    partition_expiration_days=730,
    incremental_strategy='insert_overwrite'   -- preferred for partitioned

    order_id,
    customer_id,
    product_id,
    amount_usd,

from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}

{% if is_incremental() %}

{% endif %}

# insert_overwrite incremental strategy:
# - Identifies which partitions are touched by new data
# - DELETEs those partitions
# - INSERTs the new data
# - Atomic per partition; clean re-runs

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Partitioning splits table by column value; query reads only matching partitions
  • Most common: partition by date column (daily granularity)
  • Clustering sorts within partitions by additional columns (1-4)
  • Use cluster for high-cardinality columns frequently filtered
  • require_partition_filter = TRUE forces users to filter on partition
  • partition_expiration_days auto-deletes old partitions
  • Cluster columns can change; partition column cannot (must rebuild)
  • In dbt: use insert_overwrite incremental strategy for partitioned tables
  • Proper partition + cluster = 10-1000x cost reduction on large tables

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

BigQuery's SQL dialect (GoogleSQL) is 90% standard SQL but has unique features around arrays, structs, and dates that you won't find in Postgres or Snowflake. Knowing them unlocks the most powerful aspects of BigQuery and avoids fighting the dialect when you're used to other warehouses.

STRUCT and ARRAY: first-class nested types

BigQuery's biggest dialect difference: arrays and structs everywhere. Designed for semi-structured JSON-like data without parsing.

# A STRUCT (record) is a typed nested object
SELECT 
    STRUCT('Alice' AS name, 42 AS age) AS person;
# Returns: {name: 'Alice', age: 42}

# Access fields:
SELECT person.name FROM ...

# ARRAY = ordered list of same type
SELECT [1, 2, 3, 4] AS numbers;

# ARRAY of STRUCTs (very common in BQ)
SELECT [
    STRUCT('A' AS sku, 100 AS price),
    STRUCT('B' AS sku, 200 AS price),
    STRUCT('C' AS sku, 50  AS price)
] AS line_items;

UNNEST: flatten arrays into rows

# Sample table: orders with line_items as ARRAY<STRUCT>
# | order_id | customer | line_items                                 |
# | 1        | Alice    | [{sku:A, qty:3}, {sku:B, qty:1}]            |
# | 2        | Bob      | [{sku:A, qty:2}, {sku:C, qty:5}, {sku:B,1}] |

# Flatten with UNNEST:
SELECT 
    order_id,
    customer,
    item.sku,
    item.qty
FROM orders, UNNEST(line_items) AS item;

# Result (one row per line item):
# 1 | Alice | A | 3
# 1 | Alice | B | 1
# 2 | Bob   | A | 2
# 2 | Bob   | C | 5
# 2 | Bob   | B | 1

# UNNEST with offset (array index)
SELECT order_id, item, position
FROM orders, UNNEST(line_items) AS item WITH OFFSET AS position;

Why nested data matters in BigQuery

  • GA4 export — event params are nested arrays of structs
  • Firebase data — same model
  • JSON ingestion — preserves structure
  • Avoids JOINs — related data lives inline, fast to query

BigQuery date/time functions

# Current date/time
CURRENT_DATE()
CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
CURRENT_DATETIME()

# Date arithmetic
DATE_ADD(order_date, INTERVAL 7 DAY)
DATE_SUB(order_date, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)
DATE_DIFF(end_date, start_date, DAY)

# Date truncation
DATE_TRUNC(order_date, MONTH)        -- first day of month
DATE_TRUNC(event_ts, WEEK)           -- start of week
DATE_TRUNC(order_date, YEAR)         -- Jan 1 of year

# Extracting components
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM order_date)   -- 1=Sun, 7=Sat
FORMAT_DATE('%Y-%m', order_date)     -- '2025-05'

# Note: different from Snowflake's DATEADD, DATE_TRUNC has reversed args
# Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', order_date)
# BigQuery: DATE_TRUNC(order_date, MONTH)

String functions

# Concatenation
CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)
first_name || ' ' || last_name        -- also works (ANSI standard)

# Substring
SUBSTR(email, 1, STRPOS(email, '@') - 1)   -- before @

# Case
UPPER(name), LOWER(email)

# Replace and clean
REPLACE(phone, '-', '')
REGEXP_REPLACE(text, r'\s+', ' ')       -- collapse whitespace
REGEXP_EXTRACT(url, r'utm_source=([^&]+)')

# Split
SPLIT(path, '/')                        -- returns array
SPLIT(path, '/')[OFFSET(0)]             -- first element

# Padding
LPAD(CAST(id AS STRING), 8, '0')         -- '00012345'

Window functions

# Same syntax as standard SQL
SELECT
    customer_id,
    order_id,
    order_date,
    amount,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_seq,
    LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_order_date,
    SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date 
                      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_spend
FROM fct_orders;

BigQuery-specific aggregations

# ARRAY_AGG — collect values into an array
SELECT 
    customer_id,
    ARRAY_AGG(order_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_ids,
    ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(order_id, order_date, amount) ORDER BY order_date) AS orders
FROM fct_orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

# APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT — HyperLogLog for billions of rows
SELECT 
    DATE(event_ts) AS day,
    APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(user_id) AS unique_users
FROM fct_events
GROUP BY 1;
# 100x faster than COUNT(DISTINCT) at scale; ~2% error

# APPROX_QUANTILES — fast percentiles
SELECT 
    APPROX_QUANTILES(amount, 100)[OFFSET(50)] AS median,
    APPROX_QUANTILES(amount, 100)[OFFSET(95)] AS p95
FROM fct_orders;

# STRING_AGG — join strings
SELECT 
    customer_id,
    STRING_AGG(product_name ORDER BY order_date, ', ') AS products_purchased
FROM fct_orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

JSON handling

# BigQuery has a JSON type and many JSON_ functions

# Extract field from JSON
SELECT 
    JSON_VALUE(properties, '$.user_id') AS user_id,
    JSON_VALUE(properties, '$.page.url') AS page_url
FROM events;

# Extract as different types
SELECT 
    JSON_VALUE(properties, '$.id') AS id_str,        -- always string
    SAFE_CAST(JSON_VALUE(properties, '$.amount') AS NUMERIC) AS amount
FROM events;

# JSON arrays
SELECT JSON_VALUE_ARRAY(properties, '$.tags') AS tags FROM events;

# Native JSON type (newer; better than STRING)
SELECT properties.user_id, properties.page.url FROM events
WHERE properties IS NOT NULL;

SAFE functions

# SAFE.* prefix returns NULL on error instead of failing the query
SAFE_CAST(amount_str AS NUMERIC)              -- NULL if can't cast
SAFE_DIVIDE(numerator, denominator)            -- NULL if divide by zero
SAFE.PARSE_DATE('%Y-%m-%d', date_str)         -- NULL if bad format

# Use cases:
# - Messy source data with occasional bad values
# - Don't want one bad row to kill the entire query
# - Common in staging models

QUALIFY clause

# BigQuery (and Snowflake) support QUALIFY — filter on window function results
# Avoids the "subquery to filter on ROW_NUMBER" pattern

SELECT *
FROM fct_orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) = 1;
# Returns first order per customer

# Equivalent without QUALIFY:
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS rn
    FROM fct_orders
) WHERE rn = 1;

# QUALIFY is cleaner. Use it.

# GA4 exports data to BigQuery with deeply nested arrays
# Schema includes event_params as ARRAY<STRUCT>

SELECT
    event_timestamp,
    event_name,
    user_id,
    -- Extract page_location from event_params (nested)
    (SELECT value.string_value 
     FROM UNNEST(event_params) 
     WHERE key = 'page_location') AS page_location,
    -- Extract page_title
    (SELECT value.string_value 
     FROM UNNEST(event_params) 
     WHERE key = 'page_title') AS page_title,
    -- Numeric param
    (SELECT value.int_value 
     FROM UNNEST(event_params) 
     WHERE key = 'session_engaged') AS session_engaged
FROM `project.analytics_xxx.events_*`
WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20250515' AND '20250516'
  AND event_name = 'page_view';

# This pattern (subquery on UNNEST) is everywhere in GA4 queries
# Memorize it.

WITH events AS (
    SELECT
        user_pseudo_id,
        event_timestamp,
        event_name,
        (SELECT value.string_value FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = 'page_location') AS page_url,

    FROM `project.analytics.events_*`

),

    SELECT 
        page_url,
        utm_source,
        COUNT(*) AS views,
        APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(user_pseudo_id) AS unique_visitors
    FROM events
    WHERE page_url IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY page_url, utm_source
)

SELECT *
FROM aggregated
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY utm_source ORDER BY views DESC) <= 10
ORDER BY utm_source, views DESC;

  • ARRAY_AGG collects values; APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT for big-data DISTINCT

  • QUALIFY: filter on window function results (cleaner than subquery)

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Databricks is the third major cloud warehouse you'll encounter. It's the "lakehouse" pioneer — combining data lake flexibility with warehouse-grade SQL. Knowing it makes you employable at ML-heavy companies and gives you the third tool that completes the modern warehouse trifecta.

What Databricks is (in plain terms)

Originally a managed Apache Spark platform. Evolved into a full data platform with three things working together:

  • Delta Lake — the storage format (Parquet + transaction log)
  • Compute — clusters (Spark) and SQL Warehouses (Photon)
  • Unity Catalog — governance layer (tables, lineage, permissions)
DATABRICKS' POSITIONING
"Lakehouse" = data lake's flexibility + warehouse's structure

Data lives in open Parquet files on cheap object storage (S3/ADLS/GCS).
Delta Lake adds transactions + ACID + time travel.
SQL Warehouses + Photon make queries fast.
Same data also accessible to ML and streaming workloads.

The Medallion architecture

Databricks' recommended pattern for organizing data:

┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐
│  BRONZE   │ → │  SILVER   │ → │   GOLD    │
│  raw      │   │  cleaned  │   │  business │
└───────────┘   └───────────┘   └───────────┘
   ingest         standardize     aggregate
   schema-on-     deduplicate     join
   read           join refs       business logic
   immutable      validate

# Bronze: 1:1 with source. Append-only. The "data lake" tier.
# Silver: cleaned, typed, validated. The "trusted core."  
# Gold:   business-ready. Stars/dimensions/marts.

# Maps to dbt's staging/intermediate/marts pattern almost exactly

Delta Lake basics

# A Delta table is Parquet files + a _delta_log directory
my_table/
  _delta_log/
    00000000000000000000.json  # transaction 0
    00000000000000000001.json  # transaction 1
    ...
    _last_checkpoint
  part-00000-uuid.parquet
  part-00001-uuid.parquet
  ...

# What Delta gives you over plain Parquet:
# - ACID transactions (concurrent writes safe)
# - Schema enforcement (rejects bad writes)
# - Schema evolution (add columns at write time)
# - Time travel (query historical versions)
# - MERGE / UPDATE / DELETE (impossible on plain Parquet)
# - OPTIMIZE + Z-ORDER (compact + cluster)
# - VACUUM (clean up old files)

Delta Lake SQL examples

# Create a Delta table
CREATE TABLE bronze.events (
    event_id STRING,
    user_id STRING,
    event_type STRING,
    event_ts TIMESTAMP
) USING DELTA;

# MERGE (upsert) — impossible on plain Parquet without rewriting everything
MERGE INTO silver.users AS target
USING staging.new_users AS source
ON target.user_id = source.user_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

# UPDATE / DELETE
UPDATE silver.users SET email_verified = true 
WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM verified_users);

DELETE FROM bronze.events WHERE event_ts < '2020-01-01';

# Time travel
SELECT * FROM events VERSION AS OF 5;
SELECT * FROM events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2025-05-15 00:00:00';

# See history
DESCRIBE HISTORY events;

OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER

# Small file problem: many writes = many small files = slow reads
# OPTIMIZE compacts them
OPTIMIZE silver.events;

# Z-ORDER: physically organize data by columns for efficient filtering
OPTIMIZE silver.events ZORDER BY (user_id, event_date);

# Now queries filtering on user_id or event_date skip irrelevant files
# Similar to Snowflake clustering, BigQuery clustering

# When to run:

Delta Lake's specific features (MERGE, time travel, OPTIMIZE, schema evolution) are the practical day-to-day tools you'll actually use. Knowing them lets you write efficient pipelines, recover from mistakes, and structure long-lived production tables.

Schema enforcement

Delta refuses writes whose schema doesn't match the table:

# Existing table
CREATE TABLE events (id STRING, user_id STRING, ts TIMESTAMP) USING DELTA;

# Try to write with extra column
INSERT INTO events SELECT id, user_id, ts, 'extra_col' FROM staging;
# Error: A schema mismatch detected when writing to the Delta table.

# Forces you to:
# (a) Match the schema
# (b) Explicitly evolve it
# Prevents accidental schema drift

Schema evolution

# Add new column to a write
INSERT INTO events 
SELECT id, user_id, ts, country_code 
FROM staging
-- Will fail without:
SET spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled = true;

# Or per-write (in PySpark)
df.write.mode('append').option('mergeSchema', 'true').saveAsTable('events')

# Schema changes are versioned in history
# Old data has NULL for new columns
# Add columns only; type changes / drops require explicit ALTER

MERGE — the killer feature

# Standard MERGE syntax
MERGE INTO silver.customers AS target
USING staging.customers_changes AS source
ON target.customer_id = source.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED AND source.updated_at > target.updated_at THEN
    UPDATE SET *
WHEN MATCHED AND source.is_deleted = true THEN
    DELETE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT *;

# Three actions in one atomic operation:
# - Update existing
# - Delete based on flag
# - Insert new

# Common patterns:
# - SCD Type 1: WHEN MATCHED UPDATE
# - SCD Type 2: more complex (use dbt snapshots or custom logic)
# - CDC application: source has _CHANGE_TYPE column → MERGE

Time travel mechanics

# View history
DESCRIBE HISTORY silver.events;
# Returns: version, timestamp, userId, operation, operationParameters, ...

# Query a prior version
SELECT * FROM silver.events VERSION AS OF 42;
SELECT * FROM silver.events TIMESTAMP AS OF '2025-05-15 12:00:00';

# Useful for:
# - "What did the table look like before the bad ETL?"
# - Reproducing model training data
# - Reconciling reports between dates

# Restore to prior version
RESTORE TABLE silver.events TO VERSION AS OF 41;
# Atomic; rolls back all changes since version 41

VACUUM — cleaning up

# Time travel keeps old files. To reclaim storage:
VACUUM silver.events RETAIN 168 HOURS;   -- keep 7 days

# After VACUUM, you can't time-travel earlier than retention
# Default minimum: 7 days (safety guard)
# Override with: VACUUM events RETAIN 1 HOURS (dangerous, but possible)

# Schedule weekly or monthly on production tables
# Reclaim cost: file deletion is free; you save storage costs

OPTIMIZE — compacting small files

# Each write creates new Parquet files
# Many small writes = many tiny files = slow reads

# Compact into ~1GB files
OPTIMIZE silver.events;

# Z-ORDER while compacting (for filter performance)
OPTIMIZE silver.events ZORDER BY (user_id, event_date);

# Z-ORDER:
# - Multi-column clustering (up to 4 columns)
# - Co-locates related rows in same files
# - Filter queries skip files with irrelevant ranges

# When to run:
# - After large appends (nightly batch loads)
# - Scheduled daily/weekly on hot tables
# - Or enable auto-optimize:
ALTER TABLE silver.events SET TBLPROPERTIES (
    'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite' = 'true',
    'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'true'
);

Liquid Clustering (newer alternative)

# Liquid Clustering is newer and easier than Z-ORDER + partitioning
CREATE TABLE silver.events (...)
USING DELTA
CLUSTER BY (user_id, event_date);

# Differences from Z-ORDER:
# - No partitioning needed
# - Background clustering (no manual OPTIMIZE)
# - Clustering keys can change without rewrite
# - Generally lower maintenance

# Use when starting fresh; Z-ORDER for legacy compatibility

Streaming with Delta

# Delta supports streaming reads and writes natively
# Auto Loader: structured streaming on cloud storage

# Auto Loader (Python)
from pyspark.sql.functions import *

stream = (spark.readStream
    .format('cloudFiles')
    .option('cloudFiles.format', 'json')
    .option('cloudFiles.schemaLocation', '/checkpoints/schema')
    .load('s3://raw/events/'))

# Write to Delta in streaming mode
(stream.writeStream
    .format('delta')
    .option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/events')
    .trigger(processingTime='1 minute')
    .table('bronze.events'))

# Same Delta table readable by:
# - SQL queries (analyst)
# - Batch jobs (data eng)
# - Other streams (downstream pipeline)
# All concurrent, ACID-safe

Change Data Feed (CDC)

# Enable CDC on a table
ALTER TABLE silver.customers SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true);

# Now downstream can read just CHANGES (not full snapshots)
SELECT * FROM table_changes('silver.customers', 5, 10);
# Returns rows with _change_type (insert/update_preimage/update_postimage/delete)

# Useful pattern: incremental dbt models reading CDC
# Bronze table updated → Silver reads only changes → Gold incremental rebuild

Constraints (Delta-specific)

# Add check constraints
ALTER TABLE silver.orders ADD CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount >= 0);
ALTER TABLE silver.orders ADD CONSTRAINT valid_status 
    CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'completed', 'cancelled'));

# Writes that violate constraints fail
INSERT INTO silver.orders VALUES (..., -100, ...);  -- fails

# Useful for guarding production tables against bad data
# Less heavy than dbt tests (which run after write)

Delta clone

# Shallow clone (metadata only, instant)
CREATE TABLE dev.events_test SHALLOW CLONE prod.events;

# Modifications to clone don't affect source
# Like Snowflake zero-copy clone

# Deep clone (full physical copy)
CREATE TABLE backup.events DEEP CLONE prod.events;

# Use cases:
# - Dev sandboxes (shallow)
# - Disaster recovery backups (deep)
# - Pre-deployment validation

📘 Performance tuning basics

A slow warehouse query is almost never slow because the warehouse is small. It is slow because it reads more than it needs to. Tuning is the discipline of reading less: fewer columns, fewer partitions, fewer rows recomputed, and looking at the plan before guessing.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

The cloud warehouse bills for what it reads and computes, so a slow query is also an expensive one. The four habits here fix most slow queries on Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks alike, and they are what an interviewer means by "how would you tune this".

Start with the plan, not a guess

Every warehouse shows you how it ran a query: Snowflake's Query Profile in Snowsight, BigQuery's execution details, Databricks' query profile, and EXPLAIN everywhere. Read it for three things: which columns the scan projects, whether your filter was pushed into the scan (partition or micro-partition pruning) or applied afterwards, and where the time went. A join that produced ten times the expected rows, or a scan that read every partition, is visible there in seconds.

Find the slow queries first

Snowflake keeps QUERY_HISTORY in ACCOUNT_USAGE with runtime, bytes scanned and warehouse for every statement; BigQuery has INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS with total_bytes_processed; Databricks has the Query History page. Sort by total time over the week, not by single slowest run: the dashboard query that takes eight seconds two thousand times a day matters more than the one-off that took ten minutes.

Cost discipline is the #1 skill that separates senior analytics engineers from junior. Six-figure surprise bills are real. Companies hire people specifically to manage warehouse spend. This section gives you the framework that applies across all three warehouses.

The cost-control mindset

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE
Compute should run only when there's work to do.
Storage should be only what you need.
Queries should read only the bytes they need.

📘 Security: roles, masking and access control

Warehouse security is three layers: who may see which objects (roles and grants), what they see inside a column (masking policies), and which rows they see at all (row access policies). All three are declared in SQL and audited from the warehouse's own history views.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

The correspondence team's data includes names, addresses and account details. Getting access right is what lets analysts work on the tables without seeing what they must not, keeps the auditors satisfied, and makes offboarding one REVOKE instead of a hunt.

Role-based access control

Privileges are never granted to people. They are granted to roles, and roles are granted to people (and to other roles, forming a hierarchy). A new analyst gets GRANT ROLE analyst TO USER ... and inherits everything the role can do; a leaver loses one grant. Every role needs USAGE on the warehouse it will compute on, USAGE on the database and schema, and then SELECT on the tables. GRANT ... ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA covers tables created later.

Masking and row access

A masking policy is a function attached to a column: when a query touches the column, the policy runs with the current role and returns either the value or a masked version. The table is stored once; the support admin and the analyst see different things from the same row. A row access policy is the same mechanism deciding whether a row is returned at all, typically by joining the current role to a mapping table of regions or teams. Both live on the table, so every tool, every notebook and every dbt model gets the same rule.

Least privilege, and proving it

Start every role with nothing and add what the job needs. Keep a separate role for the transformation tool (dbt) with write access to its own schemas and read access to raw, and give people read access to the marts. Then use the history: ACCESS_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY say who touched which table and when, which is both the audit trail and the way to spot a role that has more than it uses.

📘 Integrating with dbt

dbt does not care which warehouse it talks to. An adapter translates its handful of warehouse-specific operations, a profile says where to connect, and the models stay plain SQL. Getting the profile right, choosing materializations that suit each warehouse, and keeping dialect-specific SQL inside macros is what makes a project portable.

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS

The team will not stay on one warehouse forever, and the same dbt project may already run against Snowflake in production and DuckDB on a laptop. A project written the portable way survives the move; one full of hard-coded dialect does not.

Adapters and the profile

Each warehouse has an adapter package: dbt-snowflake, dbt-bigquery, dbt-databricks, dbt-duckdb. Install the one you need next to dbt-core, then describe the connection in profiles.yml: the adapter type, credentials (from environment variables, never in the file), and one output per environment. dbt debug proves the connection before anything else is attempted.

BigQuerydbt-bigqueryproject, dataset, method (oauth or service account)set partition_by and cluster_by on big models; incremental with insert_overwrite by partition
Databricksdbt-databrickshost, http_path of the SQL warehouse, token, catalog, schemaDelta tables; incremental merge; liquid_clustered_by
DuckDBdbt-duckdba file paththe same project for local development and tests

Keep the dialect inside macros

Most SQL is portable. The parts that are not, date arithmetic, string splitting, JSON access, belong in macros so a model reads {{ dbt.dateadd("day", -7, "order_date") }} and the adapter emits the right spelling. dbt_utils and dbt's own cross-database macros cover the common cases, and adapter.dispatch lets you write one macro with a per-warehouse implementation when you must. Never write DATEADD or DATE_ADD by hand in a model that might move.

Going deeper: talking about warehouses in interviews

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

You'll be in interviews soon. Knowing the cloud warehouse concepts is necessary but not sufficient — you also need to know how to TALK about them. This section gives you the patterns, questions, and STAR-format answers that consistently win warehouse-focused interviews.

Common interview questions about warehouses

"Walk me through how a cloud data warehouse works"

# Strong answer structure:

# 1. Foundational concept
"Cloud data warehouses separate storage from compute, which is the 
fundamental architectural choice that enables everything else."

# 2. Storage
"Data lives in cheap object storage — S3, GCS, Azure Blob — in 
columnar format like Parquet, often with a transaction log on top 
(like Delta or Snowflake's micro-partitions) that adds ACID."

# 3. Compute
"Compute is provisioned separately — Snowflake calls them 'virtual 
warehouses,' BigQuery has slots, Databricks has SQL Warehouses or 
clusters. You can scale compute independently of storage, run 
multiple compute clusters against the same data, and pay only 
when compute is actually running."

# 4. Why it matters
"This unlocks elastic pricing (auto-suspend = no idle cost), 
time travel (storage retains history cheaply), and analytics 
workloads that would crash a traditional OLTP database."

# Total ~45 seconds. Hits architecture, examples, and "why."

"How do you optimize a slow query in a warehouse?"

# Walk through a structured approach:

# 1. Read the query profile/plan first
"Whatever warehouse, I start by reading the query profile. In 
Snowflake that's the Query Profile tab; in BigQuery the Execution 
details; in Databricks the Spark UI. I look for the bottleneck — 
usually one of: full table scan, expensive JOIN, spillage to disk, 
or skew."

# 2. Common fixes by symptom
"For full table scan: add partition filters and column pruning.
For expensive JOIN: check that we're joining on indexed/clustered 
columns; consider broadcasting smaller tables.
For spillage: query needs more memory — upsize warehouse OR rewrite 
to be less memory-hungry (avoid huge intermediates).
For skew: redistribute the data or use skewed join hints."

# 3. The 'easy wins' that often help
"SELECT only needed columns. Use LIMIT during dev. Filter on 
partition columns. Materialize hot CTEs."

# Total ~60 seconds. Shows methodology, not just facts.

"When would you choose Snowflake vs BigQuery vs Databricks?"

# Don't say "Snowflake is best." Show maturity:

"Depends on a few factors. First, cloud strategy — if you're 
all-in on GCP, BigQuery removes friction. Second, workload mix — 
if you have heavy ML + analytics on the same data, Databricks' 
lakehouse model is compelling. Snowflake tends to be the best 
pick for SQL-heavy analytics teams who want the most polished 
experience.

Third, cost profile — BigQuery on-demand is great for bursty 
workloads with unpredictable usage; Snowflake/Databricks charge 
for time so they reward predictable patterns.

Fourth, team skills — existing Spark expertise points to 
Databricks. SQL-first analysts adapt fastest to Snowflake.

For most analytics teams I'd actually default to Snowflake — 
best UX, most jobs available, dbt support is excellent. But the 
right answer depends on the company's specific context."

"How do you control warehouse costs?"

# The five-lever framework:

"Five main levers. First, short auto-suspend on every warehouse — 
60 seconds, not the 10-minute default. Single biggest win.

Second, right-size warehouses. Most teams oversize. A query 
doesn't cost less on a bigger warehouse — it runs faster but 
proportionally more expensive. I downsize and only upsize when 
spillage forces it.

Third, incremental dbt models instead of full rebuilds. Easy 
20-50% savings on large fact tables.

Fourth, partition and cluster heavy tables. Pruning lets queries 
skip 90%+ of data.

Fifth, monitor runaway queries — query history reveals the top 
20 most expensive queries. Optimize those first.

Plus hard guardrails: resource monitors with budget caps, 
statement timeouts to kill runaways, partition_filter_required 
on critical tables."

"Tell me about a time you reduced warehouse costs"

# STAR format, with numbers:

# Situation: 
"At my last role, our Snowflake bill grew from $5k to $18k/month 
over six months. Leadership wanted to know why and asked me to 
investigate."

# Task:
"I had two weeks to identify causes and propose fixes."

# Action:
"I started with the query history and ran an audit. Found three 
big issues:
1. A BI tool was auto-refreshing every 5 minutes against a 
   warehouse with no auto-suspend, costing $3k/month for 
   essentially-idle reports.
2. Our nightly dbt build was full-refresh; converting 5 key fact 
   tables to incremental cut runtime from 90 to 25 minutes.
3. Three analysts had personal sandboxes running at L-size; XS 
   was plenty for their workload.

I implemented the fixes over a week, then monitored for 
regressions."

# Result:
"Cut spend back to $9k/month — a $9k savings, or 50%. 
Documented the patterns in our team's onboarding doc so new 
hires don't repeat the mistakes."

# Total: 90 seconds. Specific, quantified, shows methodology + impact.

"Explain partitioning and clustering"

# Get the distinction right:

"Both reduce the data a query reads, but they work differently.

Partitioning splits a table into physically-separate segments by 
a column's value — typically a date. Queries filtering on that 
column skip non-matching partitions entirely. So 'WHERE order_date 
= 2025-05-15' might read 50MB instead of 5TB.

Clustering sorts data WITHIN partitions (or within the entire 
table) by additional columns. It doesn't skip whole partitions 
but skips blocks within them. So you'd partition by date AND 
cluster by customer_id for a workload that filters on both.

In BigQuery you partition on dates (max 4000 partitions) and 
cluster on up to 4 columns. In Snowflake, micro-partitions are 
automatic; you 'cluster' on the columns to optimize for. 
Databricks uses Z-ORDER or the newer Liquid Clustering.

Rule of thumb: partition by what you ALWAYS filter on (usually 
a date). Cluster by what you OFTEN filter or join on (IDs, 
categories)."

"What's the difference between ELT and ETL?"

"Extract, Transform, Load vs Extract, Load, Transform — order of 
operations matters.

ETL was the old pattern: transform data in a dedicated tool 
(Informatica, SSIS, Python scripts) before loading into the 
warehouse. Made sense when warehouses were expensive — you didn't 
want to compute on them more than necessary.

ELT is the modern pattern: load raw data into the warehouse first, 
transform with SQL (typically via dbt). Made sense once cloud 
warehouses became cheap to compute on AND infinitely scalable.

Benefits of ELT:
- Raw data preserved; you can re-transform anytime
- Transformations are version-controlled SQL (vs proprietary tools)
- One tool to learn (warehouse) instead of two
- Easier to debug (you can inspect raw data)

ETL still appears in:
- Streaming pipelines where you need to enrich before warehouse
- Compliance scenarios where PII can't enter warehouse raw
- Heavy unstructured data where SQL isn't the right tool

90% of new pipelines I'd build today are ELT."

Things to mention without prompting

These signal seniority when you naturally weave them in:

  • Time travel as a debugging tool — "I once recovered from a bad dbt run by cloning the table AT(timestamp) before the bad run"
  • The cost of SELECT * — "Avoiding SELECT * isn't just a style preference; it defeats the column-pruning advantage"
  • Partition_filter_required — "I'd require partition filter on any fact table over 100GB"
  • Cross-database portability via dbt — "I keep transformations in dbt so we're not locked into one warehouse"
  • The chatter-vs-action gap in cost — "Auto-suspend at 60s is the single best ROI change you can make"

Red flags to avoid

  • "I prefer X warehouse" without explaining what workloads
  • Confusing partition with index (warehouses generally don't have row-level indexes)
  • "Bigger warehouse = faster = better" (cost matters too)
  • Not knowing your warehouse's pricing model
  • Talking only about technology, not business outcomes

Mock interview yourself

For each of these, write out (or speak out loud) a 60-second answer:

  1. How does a cloud data warehouse work?
  2. How would you optimize a slow query?
  3. How would you reduce warehouse costs?
  4. When would you use Snowflake vs BigQuery vs Databricks?
  5. Explain partitioning vs clustering
  6. What's ELT vs ETL?
  7. Walk me through dbt's role in your stack
  8. What's the modern data stack?
★ THE INTERVIEW WIN

Senior interviewers can spot rehearsed answers a mile away — but they LOVE candidates who clearly know the material and answer with specific examples. The way to bridge: rehearse the FRAMEWORK, then fill in with YOUR examples in real time. "Five cost levers" + "I once saved $9k/mo by..." is unbeatable.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Cloud warehouse story: storage/compute separation → elastic + ACID + time travel
  • Query optimization: profile first, then partition filter / column pruning / right-size
  • Choosing a warehouse: depends on cloud, team, workloads, budget — not "best"
  • Cost: 5 levers (auto-suspend, sizing, incremental, partitioning, runaways) + guardrails
  • STAR format: situation, task, action, result with specific numbers
  • Partition + cluster distinction matters; explain both clearly
  • ELT replaced ETL because warehouses got cheap and dbt got good
  • Mention time travel, SELECT * cost, dbt portability without prompting
  • Practice 60-second answers out loud for top 8 questions
